newsitem.title: USA: Vietnam vet thinks McVeigh "very possibly" guilty.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam vet thinks McVeigh "very possibly" guilty.

text.p: A wounded Vietnam War veteran said Wednesday he thought accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was "very possibly" guilty but would try to set aside his prejudices if chosen to sit on the jury.

On the eighth day of jury selection, the former soldier said he blew up booby traps and bunkers in Vietnam and used explosives including ammonium nitrate fuel oil bombs of the type prosecutors allege were used in the Oklahoma bombing.
He said he thought the 28-year-old Gulf War veteran was "very possibly" guilty and believed prosecutors were "coming up with fairly good circumstantial evidence" against him.

"From what I understand, he's a little anti-government, a little on the radical side," said the man, a manufacturing worker who, like other potential jurors, was identified only by a number and sat behind a screen shielding him from the view of most spectators.
Despite his views, he said he could be impartial if chosen to sit in judgment of McVeigh.

Forty-six people have been quizzed during the slow process of choosing a jury to try McVeigh, accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah building April 19, 1995, killing 168 people. He pleaded not guilty but faces the death penalty if convicted.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch earlier excused a man who did not meet the one-year residency requirement in Colorado to sit on the jury. Matsch apologised for failing to notice this in the man's jury questionnaire.

He was only the third person publicly excused during jury selection. A woman was dismissed Tuesday because Matsch said she could not be impartial and another woman was excused last week because she suffered from stress.
In a letter published in an Oklahoma weekly newspaper Wednesday, McVeigh accused the Federal Bureau of Investigation of burning young children alive at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas.

McVeigh said in the letter, which he sent to the Oklahoma Gazette last November, that FBI agents murdered the Branch Davidians and covered up the truth when the Waco compound went up in flames on April 19, 1993.

"The public never saw the Davidians' home video of their cute babies, adorable children, loving mothers or protective fathers," McVeigh said. "Nor did they see pictures of the charred remains of children's bodies. Therefore they didn't care when these families died a slow, torturous death as they were gassed and burned alive at the hands of the FBI."

Branch Davidian leader David Koresh and at least 80 of his followers were killed by flames or gunfire when the FBI raided their compound at the end of a 51-day siege. Prosecutors allege McVeigh took revenge by blowing up the federal building on the second anniversary of the Branch Davidian fire.
Nineteen children died in the Oklahoma City bombing.

The defence fears media reports about the Oklahoma City bombing will prejudice jurors against McVeigh. But a health care worker interviewed Wednesday said she felt pre-trial publicity had not affected the bombing case as much as it did the trial of former football star O.J. Simpson, who was acquitted of two murders in a sensational 1995 trial.

The woman was one of a handful of potential jurors who said they believed Simpson was innocent. "It seems like every channel they had on TV they were always talking about it," she said. "This case is a little quieter and people are trying to be calmer about it."
